name.text: Classifying a function as Even, Odd, or Neither

questiontext.text:
Consider the function

\[ k(x) = \dfrac{ {@numer@} }{ {@denom@} }. \]

(a) Find \(k(-x)\), simplifying each power of \(-x\).

\( k(-x) = \) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Hence classify \(k(x)\) as even, odd, or neither.

\( k(x) \) is [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
A function is even if \(k(-x) = k(x)\) for every \(x\), and odd if \(k(-x) = -k(x)\) for every \(x\). To classify \(k\), substitute \(-x\) for every occurrence of \(x\) and compare the result with \(k(x)\) and \(-k(x)\).

A term with an even power of \(x\) (including a constant, which is \(x^0\)) is unchanged when \(x\) is replaced by \(-x\), because \((-x)^{\text{even}}=x^{\text{even}}\). A term with an odd power of \(x\) changes sign, because \((-x)^{\text{odd}}=-x^{\text{odd}}\). The denominator here has only even powers, so it does not change.

\[ k(-x) = {@fnegx@}. \]
  • If \(k(-x)=k(x)\), the function is even.
  • If \(k(-x)=-k(x)\), the function is odd.
  • Otherwise, it is neither.
[[if test="is_even"]]

Every term of \(k\) has an even power of \(x\), so \(k(-x) = k(x)\) and \(k(x)\) is even. Its graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis.

[[elif test="is_odd"]]

Every term of the numerator has an odd power of \(x\) and the denominator is even, so \(k(-x) = -k(x)\) and \(k(x)\) is odd. Its graph is unchanged by a half-turn about the origin.

[[else]]

The numerator has both even and odd powers of \(x\), so \(k(-x)\) is neither \(k(x)\) nor \(-k(x)\): \(k(x)\) is neither even nor odd. Its graph has neither kind of symmetry.

[[/if]]

The graph of \(y = k(x)\) shows this symmetry.

questiondescription.text: Grade 11 Functions, Section 16.6 (Even and Odd Functions). The scenario (even/odd/neither) and the model answer for k(-x) are both derived by the CAS from the same general expression. Diagnoses the common errors of not substituting -x at all, flipping the sign of every term including even powers, missing the sign change of an odd-power term, and wrongly flipping the sign of the constant term. The graph is shown in the worked solution only, because in the question it would give away part (b).

node.description: Diagnostic A: flipped every sign (even k) or did not substitute (odd or neither k)

truefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(scenario=0)"]]

Not every term changes sign. Only terms with an odd power of \(x\) change sign; terms with an even power (like \(x^2\), \(x^4\) or a constant) stay the same, because \((-x)^{\text{even}}=x^{\text{even}}\).

[[else]]

This is identical to \(k(x)\). It looks as if you did not substitute \(-x\) for \(x\). Replace every \(x\) with \((-x)\) and simplify each power.

[[/if]]

node.description: Diagnostic B: missed the sign change of the x term (odd k) or flipped the constant (even or neither k)

truefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(scenario=1)"]]

Check the term in \(x\). Every term with an odd power of \(x\) changes sign, and \(x = x^1\) is an odd power, just like \(x^3\).

[[else]]

Check the constant term again. A constant is \(x^0\), which has an even power, so it never changes sign when \(x\) is replaced by \(-x\).

[[/if]]

falsefeedback.text: That is not equivalent to \(k(-x)\). Substitute \(-x\) for every \(x\) in \(k(x)\), in the numerator and the denominator, and simplify each power of \(-x\) term by term.
Compare \(k(-x)\) with \(k(x)\): if they are identical, the function is even; if \(k(-x)=-k(x)\), it is odd; otherwise it is neither.
